154,820 km2: the Austrian lands plus the Burgundian Netherlands (Low Countries 202 cells, Flanders 77), and only one cell each of Artois and Franche-Comte. 'Upon the death of Mary of Burgundy in 1482, her substantial possessions including the Burgundian Netherlands passed to her son, Philip the Handsome', with Maximilian as regent 1482-1493. The Treaty of Arras (23 December 1482) treated Franche-Comte and Artois as Margaret's dowry, so leaving them out is right. The Hungarian capture of Vienna (1485) is drawn as a hatched occupation, not as a smaller shape. No area on the Habsburg Netherlands page to compare.

47,354 km2: Lower Austria and Styria (53,109 km2 of the 1481 shape, 13.3-16.9E, 46.4-48.9N) are cut out and the Netherlands leave for Cliopatria's Habsburg Monarchy row. The pages opened give the Hungarian side only in part: Matthias 'occupied Lower Austria between 1482 and 1487', took fortresses in Styria and Carinthia in 1479 and Mautern in Styria and Sankt Polten in Lower Austria in 1481, adopted the title Duke of Austria in 1487; the war page says only that the Black Army 'conquered most of the Lower Austrian territories', and 'After Matthias Corvinus died ... on 6 April 1490, Frederick was able to regain the Austrian lands without serious fight'. Occupied land stays the owner's and is hatched (ledger occupation 1485-1490), so the shape is the full Austrian lands of 1492; Styria and Carinthia beyond the named fortresses are not documented as occupied.

correction.text: the Austrian lands in full; Lower Austria occupied by Matthias Corvinus 1485 to August 1490 (hatched)

The Burgundian lands, including Artois and Franche-Comte after the Treaty of Senlis (1493), are in Cliopatria's Habsburg Monarchy row 1487-1506 (70,612 km2 in 1497), not here.

ledger.note: 1260: the Habsburg counts hold their home lands around Habsburg Castle in the Aargau. Habsburg Castle was 'built in the 1020s in present-day Switzerland by Radbot of Klettgau'; early holdings included countship rights in the Zürichgau, Aargau and Thurgau (page, paraphrased). The first documented use of the name is 1108. Cliopatria's row begins in 1260; the page gives the dynasty's origin, not a 1260 foundation.

region.text: countship rights in Zurichgau, Aargau, and Thurgau; Habsburg Castle in the Aargau

ledger.note: 1264: Rudolf seizes the Kyburg estates. He seized the estates of his childless maternal uncle, Count Hartmann IV of Kyburg, after 'the death of his childless maternal uncle Count Hartmann IV of Kyburg in 1264'. The page does not say where they lay; Cliopatria's shapes show no matching change.

region.text: the estates of his childless maternal uncle Count Hartmann IV of Kyburg

ledger.note: 1276: the Habsburgs take Vienna as their seat. The infobox of the Duchy of Austria gives Vienna as capital for the Habsburg period; Rudolf took the dominion in 1276. Habsburg Castle in the Aargau stays the ancestral seat.

1276: Ottokar II of Bohemia gives up Austria and its neighbours to Rudolf. In November 1276 Ottokar was compelled to cede the four provinces to royal administration (paraphrased), after war was declared in June 1276; the Duchy of Austria page says Rudolf 'took over the dominion as the first monarch of the Habsburg dynasty in 1276'. The four provinces are named from the infobox span 'Duke of Carinthia and Carniola 1276-1286' and the Austria and Styria enfeoffment of 1282, not by the sentence. Ottokar fell at the Marchfeld on 26 August 1278.

region.text: the four provinces ceded to royal administration

ledger.note: December 1282: Rudolf makes Austria and Styria hereditary duchies of his house. At the Augsburg Hoftag Rudolf invested his sons Albert and Rudolf II with the duchies of Austria and Styria (paraphrased); the Duchy of Austria page has 'granted the Austrian domains to his sons Albert and Rudolf II at the 1282 Diet of Augsburg' and primogeniture in the Treaty of Rheinfelden (1283). The House of Habsburg page instead has 'the Georgenberg Pact of 1286'. No land changes drawn: the land was already Habsburg-held since 1276.

1286: Carinthia goes to Count Meinhard. 'In 1286, King Rudolf fully invested Albert's father-in-law Count Meinhard with the Duchy of Carinthia'; the infobox ends Rudolf as 'Duke of Carinthia and Carniola' in 1286, and the Duchy of Austria page says Carinthia with the March of Carniola had first been ceded to the House of Gorizia (paraphrased). Cliopatria's shape drops both in 1294. Reviewer (eu-09-d): counterpart is the Tyrol line of the Meinhardiner: 'When their sons divided their estate in 1271, the elder Meinhard II took Tyrol' and 'he received the Duchy of Carinthia with the Carniolan march in 1286' (County of Tyrol).

region.text: the Duchy of Carinthia, invested to Count Meinhard (with Carniola, per the infobox span to 1286)

ledger.note: 1311: the Habsburgs take over Savinja. 'In 1311, they took over Savinja.' The page names no counterpart.

region.text: in 1311, they took over Savinja

ledger.note: 1335: Carinthia and Carniola fall to the Habsburgs. The Duchy of Austria page: Carinthia with the March of Carniola 'came under Habsburg rule in 1335'; the House of Habsburg page: 'after the death of Henry in 1335, they assumed power in Carniola and Carinthia'. Cliopatria's shape adds them in 1344. Reviewer (eu-09-d): Henry held Carinthia as count of Tyrol ('Henry II 1295–1335, son of Meinhard II, also Duke of Carinthia', County of Tyrol), so the counterpart is county-of-tyrol.

region.text: Carinthia with the March of Carniola, which had first been ceded to the House of Gorizia

ledger.note: 1363: Margaret Maultasch leaves Tyrol to Rudolf IV of Austria. She 'bequeathed the county to Rudolph IV of Habsburg, Duke of Austria in 1363'; the Duchy of Austria page agrees ('ceded to Duke Rudolf IV of Austria by Countess Margaret in 1363'). The House of Habsburg page has 'in 1369, they succeeded his daughter Margaret in Tyrol'. Reviewer (eu-09-d): counterpart is duchy-of-bavaria, whose dossier draws Tyrol 1342-1362 (Margaret and Louis V 'ruled Tyrol and Brandenburg in personal union'; 'Louis V died in 1361, followed by Margaret's son Meinhard III two years later', County of Tyrol) and records the 1363 loss to house-of-habsburg.

region.text: bequeathed the county to Rudolph IV of Habsburg, Duke of Austria in 1363

ledger.note: 1374: the Habsburgs reach Istria. 'After the death of Albert III of Gorizia in 1374, they gained a foothold at Pazin.'

region.text: they gained a foothold at Pazin

ledger.note: 25 September 1379: the Treaty of Neuberg divides the Habsburg lands between two lines. 'The separation of the so-called Albertinian and Leopoldian family lines on 25 September 1379': Albert's line keeps Austria proper, Leopold's takes Inner Austria (Styria, Carinthia, Carniola), Tyrol and Further Austria. Internal to the dynasty: one state, one colour. The Duchy of Austria page adds a further split of the Leopoldian line in 1402, the Tyrol page one in 1406.
1382: Trieste comes to the Habsburgs. 'Trieste in 1382.' The page names no counterpart; the commune is named as the party.

region.text: Trieste in 1382

ledger.note: 1402: about 1,300 km2 appear in the shape. Page silent on the land: the Further Austria page says only that Frederick IV had been regent in Further Austria since 1402. Region taken from Cliopatria's 1402 shape against its 1395 shape (9.0-10.5E, 46.6-48.0N).

region.text: the cells Cliopatria adds in 1402; no page opened dates them

ledger.note: 1415: the Swiss conquer the Aargau. 'The Aargau was conquered in 1415'; the House of Habsburg page: 'Habsburg Castle itself was finally lost to the Swiss in 1415'. The Fricktal around Rheinfelden and Laufenburg stays Habsburg to 1797 (Further Austria page).

region.text: the Aargau was conquered in 1415 (the Fricktal excepted)

ledger.note: December 1437: Albert V becomes king of Hungary. The infobox gives his Hungarian reign from 18 December 1437 (crowned 1 January 1438); he is also crowned king of Bohemia on 29 June 1438 but 'was unable to obtain possession of the country'. Drawn as a personal union in the lighter tint; Cliopatria draws nothing for 1437-1439.

region.text: Albert was crowned king of Hungary on 1 January 1438

ledger.note: 27 October 1439: Albert dies at Neszmely; his reign as king of Hungary and of the Romans ends, and Ladislaus the Posthumous succeeds as duke of Austria.

region.text: he died on 27 October 1439 at Neszmely

ledger.note: 29 January 1453: the Hungarian Diet recognises Ladislaus. 'The Diet of Hungary acknowledged Ladislaus' position as the lawful king' at Pressburg, after the regency of John Hunyadi (elected 6 June 1446) ended in early 1453. Drawn as a personal union, not direct Habsburg land: Ladislaus was a minor.

region.text: the Diet of Hungary acknowledged Ladislaus' position as the lawful king

ledger.note: 28 October 1453: Ladislaus is crowned king of Bohemia at Prague. 'Poděbrady remained in full control of the government' (regency 1453-1457).

region.text: crowned king of Bohemia in Prague on 28 October 1453

ledger.note: 23 November 1457: Ladislaus dies at Prague and the union of Hungary with the Habsburg house ends; Matthias Corvinus is elected about two months later.

region.text: Ladislaus unexpectedly died on 23 November 1457

ledger.note: 23 November 1457: Ladislaus dies and Bohemia leaves the union; 'George of Poděbrady was elected king of Bohemia on 3 March 1458'. Austria goes jointly to Frederick III and Albert VI.

region.text: George of Poděbrady was elected king of Bohemia on 3 March 1458

ledger.note: 1460: the Swiss take the Thurgau. 'The Thurgau in 1460' was conquered, like the Aargau, when the Swiss profited from Habsburg weakness (paraphrased; the page names the Thurgau among the conquests of that kind). Cliopatria's Habsburg shapes never contain the Thurgau, so no drawn cell changes; a gap-filler should open a page on the Thurgau.

region.text: the Thurgau in 1460

ledger.note: 1469: Sigismund pawns Further Austria to Charles the Bold. 'From 1469 to 1474 Archduke Sigismund gave large parts in pawn to the Burgundian duke Charles the Bold.' The page does not list the parts; Alsace and the Breisgau around Freiburg are my reading.

region.text: large parts in pawn to the Burgundian duke Charles the Bold

ledger.note: 1474: the Burgundian pawn of Further Austria ends ('From 1469 to 1474').

region.text: From 1469 to 1474 Archduke Sigismund gave large parts in pawn

ledger.note: 1477: Matthias Corvinus invades Lower Austria. 'Matthias invaded Lower Austria and imposed a blockade on Vienna' after declaring war on Frederick III.

region.text: Matthias invaded Lower Austria and imposed a blockade on Vienna

ledger.note: August 1477: Maximilian marries Mary of Burgundy while France holds her lands. 'On 19 August 1477 the wedding took place, thereby joining the houses of Burgundy and Habsburg together'; 'during the first months of 1477, almost all of the aforementioned territories (except Flanders) were successfully seized', and the County of Burgundy 'remained in French hands'. The House of Habsburg page dates the wedding 16 August 1477. Artois and Franche-Comte are the zone named by the Treaty of Arras; the page does not list the seized lands one by one.

region.text: the Burgundian territories seized by France in 1477 (Artois and the County of Burgundy)

ledger.note: 1 December 1477: peace between Matthias and Frederick III ('which was signed on 1 December 1477'); Frederick confirms Matthias as ruler of Bohemia.

region.text: the peace signed on 1 December 1477

ledger.note: 1481: Matthias seizes Sankt Polten and Mautern. He 'seized the town of Mautern in Styria and Sankt Pölten in Lower Austria' for a loan of 100,000 florins; the page says he 'occupied Lower Austria between 1482 and 1487'.

region.text: seized the town of Mautern in Styria and Sankt Pölten in Lower Austria

ledger.note: 1482: the Burgundian Netherlands pass to the Habsburgs. 'Upon the death of Mary of Burgundy in 1482, her substantial possessions including the Burgundian Netherlands passed to her son, Philip the Handsome'; Maximilian is regent 1482-1493. Cliopatria's Duchy of Burgundy row ends in 1481. The Maximilian page dates Mary's death to a riding accident on 27 March 1482.

region.text: her substantial possessions including the Burgundian Netherlands

ledger.note: 23 December 1482: the Treaty of Arras. 'The Treaty of Arras was signed on 23 December 1482': Maximilian recognises the French annexation of the Duchy of Burgundy and 'several other territories'; Franche-Comte and Artois 'were treated as Margaret's dowry', i.e. left under French control until 1493.

region.text: Franche-Comte and Artois treated as Margaret's dowry

ledger.note: 1485: the Hungarian campaign turns into an occupation of Lower Austria (bridging entry; the pages give no date for the end of the 1481 phase).

region.text: Lower Austria, contested since 1481

ledger.note: 1485: the Black Army takes Vienna. The war page lists the 'Siege of Vienna (1485)' and records 'Black Army captures Vienna'; Wiener Neustadt falls in 1487 ('captured in 1487'); Matthias adopts the title Duke of Austria in 1487. No month on the pages; the Matthias page has 'occupied Lower Austria between 1482 and 1487'.

region.text: the Black Army captures Vienna and conquered most of the Lower Austrian territories

ledger.note: 1487: Cliopatria moves the Burgundian Netherlands from the House of Habsburg row to its Habsburg Monarchy row (1487-1506). Bridging entry: the Habsburg Netherlands page has Maximilian as regent 1482-1493 and no change of ruler in 1487.

region.text: the Netherlands in Cliopatria's Habsburg Monarchy row

ledger.note: 1490: Tyrol and Further Austria are reunited under Maximilian. Archduke Sigismund 'renounced Tyrol and Further Austria' in his favour; 'Maximilian's mediation led to a reconciliation and a reunited dynastic rule in 1490'. Internal to the dynasty; no land changes drawn.

August 1490: Vienna is recovered. 'Maximilian entered Vienna, already evacuated by the Hungarians, in August 1490', after Matthias died on 6 April 1490; the Peace of Pressburg (1491) 'arranged for the return of Matthias' conquests'.

region.text: Maximilian entered Vienna, already evacuated by the Hungarians, in August 1490

ledger.note: 1500: the Gorizia inheritance. 'In 1500 he also acquired the remaining Gorizia (Gorz) territories around Lienz and the Puster Valley'; the Maximilian page has the inheritance contract negotiated 1497-1498. The Gorizia disc is Cliopatria's: its 1502 shape adds cells at 13.4-13.7E, 45.8-46.4N.

region.text: the remaining Gorizia (Gorz) territories around Lienz and the Puster Valley

ledger.note: 30 July 1505: Maximilian takes the Kufstein territory. 'The emperor took the territory around Kufstein for himself as reward for his mediation' at the Diet of Cologne; he 'took Kufstein, receiving the surrender of Rattenberg, Schwaz, Zillertal' and Kitzbuhel is among the places surrendered. Infobox: territories ceded to the County of Tyrol; the rest of Bavaria-Landshut goes to Bavaria-Munich and Palatinate-Neuburg.

region.text: the territory around Kufstein, with Rattenberg and Kitzbuhel

ledger.note: 1507: the Burgundian lands are back in the House row. Philip the Handsome died in 1506 and 'Charles ... succeeded his father as Duke in 1506, when he was six years old'; Margaret of Austria governs 1507-1530. The Treaty of Senlis (1493) had returned Artois, Franche-Comte and Charolais to Philip (War of the Burgundian Succession page: France 'ceded' them); Cliopatria draws them in its Habsburg Monarchy row from 1497 and in this row from 1507.

region.text: the Burgundian Netherlands, Artois and Franche-Comte under Margaret of Austria

ledger.note: 1515: Cliopatria's House of Habsburg row ends; its Habsburg Monarchy row carries the hereditary lands from 1516. 'Attaining full age in 1515, Charles went on to rule his Burgundian heritage' and 'In 1516, Charles became the king of Spain'; Charles V was elected emperor in 1519 (House of Habsburg). The dynasty goes on; this is a break in the data, not an end of the house.

region.text: the Habsburg hereditary lands, continued by the Habsburg Monarchy row from 1516

wars.name: Rudolf I's war with Ottokar II of Bohemia (Battle on the Marchfeld)

zones.text: the four provinces ceded to royal administration

wars.outcome: War declared June 1276; in November 1276 Ottokar cedes the four provinces to royal administration; on 26 August 1278 Ottokar is defeated and killed at the Battle on the Marchfeld (paraphrased).
wars.note: The page gives no fighting between 1276 and 1278, so no contest is recorded; the land changes hands by cession in 1276.

wars.name: Habsburg wars with the Swiss (Morgarten, Sempach, Naefels, the Aargau)
wars.outcome: Swiss victories over the Habsburgs at Morgarten (1315), Sempach (1386) and Naefels (1388); the Swiss conquer the Aargau in 1415 and the Thurgau in 1460. The Old Zurich War (1436-1450) saw Zurich allied with the Habsburg dukes before it rejoined the confederacy.
wars.note: The page gives 1315 as 'a victory against the Habsburgs in 1315'; no month for any battle. Losses before 1415 (Zug, Lucerne, Zurich) are undated on the pages opened.

wars.name: Austrian-Hungarian War (1477-1488)

zones.text: Matthias invaded Lower Austria and imposed a blockade on Vienna

wars.outcome: Hungarian victory: the Black Army captures Vienna (1485) and Wiener Neustadt (1487); 'In 1490, Matthias' unexpected death led to a reversal of his gains' and the Peace of Pressburg (1491) arranged the return of the conquests.
wars.note: Peace of 1 December 1477 (Matthias Corvinus page) ended the first phase; fighting resumed from 1481. Styria and Carinthia beyond the fortresses named for 1479 and 1481 are not documented as occupied.

wars.name: War of the Burgundian Succession

zones.text: Franche-Comte and Artois treated as Margaret's dowry

wars.outcome: France annexes the Duchy of Burgundy and several other territories; the Treaty of Arras (23 December 1482) leaves Artois and Franche-Comte with France as Margaret's dowry; the Treaty of Senlis (1493) returns them to Philip the Handsome.
wars.note: Guinegate, 7 August 1479: French troops 'defeated by an army of Flemish and Habsburg forces'.

wars.name: War of the Succession of Landshut
wars.outcome: Victory of Bavaria-Munich; Maximilian arbitrates at Cologne on 30 July 1505 and keeps the Kufstein territory for the County of Tyrol; Palatinate-Neuburg is created for the heirs of Bavaria-Landshut.
wars.note: George of Bavaria-Landshut died on 1 December 1503. The Maximilian page mentions only 'Bavaria dispute in 1504'.

wars.name: Maximilian I's war on Venice (League of Cambrai)
wars.outcome: 'One particularly humiliating campaign occurred in 1508,' when Maximilian attacked Venice and was blocked; 'He acknowledged French control of Milan in 1515.' No border of the Habsburg shape moves on the page.
wars.note: The Maximilian page dates neither the League of Cambrai nor an end of the war.

certainty.note: A dynasty's scattered holdings (Aargau, Alsace, Austria, Tyrol, the Istrian outposts); the dukedoms of Austria and Styria have defined edges but the pages give no surveyed lines. The Swiss frontier is soft until the 1415 and 1460 conquests.
The French frontier of the Burgundian lands is treaty-fixed (Arras, 23 December 1482; Senlis, 1493) and could be drawn sharp; every other frontier stays soft.

notes:
Cliopatria's House of Habsburg row (1260-1515, 31 shapes) is the Habsburg dynasty's hereditary lands; the same dynasty is also drawn by the Habsburg Monarchy row (1487-1805), which carries the Burgundian Netherlands in 1487-1506 and has a gap in 1507-1515 that this row fills (this row holds the Austrian lands in 1487-1506, and both in 1482-1486 and 1507-1515). I kept Cliopatria's split and recorded it as split (1487) and merge (1507) at confidence 1-2; the orchestrator should decide whether the two rows are one state (different Wikidata ids: Q65968 and the Monarchy's).

Corrections: (1) Cliopatria's Kingdom of Hungary row has a gap 1450-1458 and its Kingdom of Bohemia row a gap 1453-1458, and fills them with the House of Habsburg shapes of 1450 and 1453 (432k and 561k km2): Hungary and Bohemia as direct Habsburg land; the pages show regencies (Hunyadi, Podebrady) and a minor king, so I drew the Austrian lands and put the two kingdoms in as vassal (personal-union) tints 1453-1457 (the regions use the kingdoms' last shapes before the gaps, Hungary 1449 and Bohemia 1452; the eu-15 dossiers of those kingdoms must decide how to draw their own gap years and Hungary 1450-1452) (and Hungary 1437-1439 under Albert V, which Cliopatria omits). (2) Cliopatria drops half the Aargau in 1333; the page dates the Swiss conquest to 1415; I added the Aargau back for 1333-1414. (3) Carinthia and Carniola: lost 1286 (Cliopatria 1294), regained 1335 (Cliopatria 1344). (4) The Hungarian occupation of Lower Austria 1485-1490 is a hatched occupation, not a smaller state; Cliopatria's 1487-1491 shape (47k km2) removes Lower Austria and Styria altogether. (5) 1276: the four provinces are Rudolf's by cession in November 1276, Cliopatria starts them in 1279.

Pages disagree: Austria and Styria enfeoffed in December 1282 (Rudolf, Duchy of Austria) versus 'Georgenberg Pact of 1286' (House of Habsburg); Tyrol 1363 (County of Tyrol, Duchy of Austria) versus 1369 (House of Habsburg); wedding of Maximilian 16 August 1477 (House of Habsburg) versus 19 August 1477 (War of the Burgundian Succession, Maximilian I). Page silent: the 1402 cells (about 1,300 km2), the six scattered cells of 1440, the counterpart of the 1311 Savinja gain, Zurich/Lucerne/Zug before 1415, the Thurgau as Habsburg land before 1460, the month of Vienna's fall in 1485, the Styrian and Carinthian extent of Matthias's conquests. Thin pages: Further Austria, Austrian-Hungarian War.

Page budget: 14 pages used, no page failed. Not opened for lack of budget: Frederick III, Albert VI and Sigismund (1457-1490), the Treaty of Senlis page, Vorarlberg acquisitions (Feldkirch 1375, Bludenz 1394, Bregenz 1451), the Old Zurich War, Gorizia, Carinthia. Keyframes marked ok rest on the House of Habsburg page where no dated sentence bears on them.

Counterparts needing dossiers: county-of-gorizia (Gorizia/Gorz, to 1500), county-of-tyrol (Meinhardiner Tyrol, to 1363). Gazetteer names used that the gazetteer lacks: Kyburg, Pazin, Savinja, Lienz, Kufstein, Rattenberg, Kitzbuhel.
